title: Packing before the rains
note: Fictional patient. Values are illustrative and follow the module text; they are not targets. PhilHealth rules are as stated in the module and must be confirmed on the date of service. The attending nephrologist and the patient decide every step.
intro:
You are the internal medicine resident on the renal service of a provincial hospital in Tarlac. Mr. Arnel Soriano, 48, a jeepney driver with chronic kidney disease (CKD) from chronic glomerulonephritis, is on the medical ward for cellulitis of the leg. His estimated glomerular filtration rate (eGFR) is 16 mL/min/1.73 m², and the Kidney Failure Risk Equation (KFRE) gives a 2-year risk of kidney failure of 47%. He feels well, eats well and drives every day. He is right-handed.

He lives with his wife, Liza, 44, and two teenage children. Your hospital runs an in-center hemodialysis (HD) unit, but no peritoneal dialysis (PD) program and no transplant service. The nearest transplant center is in Metro Manila.

n1.scene: The intern, Dr. Bea Manalo, needs blood for cultures and five more days of intravenous antibiotic. The best veins are in his left forearm, and she suggests a peripherally inserted central catheter (PICC) in the left arm “so we stop poking him.”

choices.text: Fine. A PICC in the left arm is kinder than five days of needle sticks.
choices.feedback: A PICC can damage the veins that a future fistula will need. The module asks you to avoid PICCs in advanced CKD unless the attending agrees.
choices.then: The charge nurse reminds you of the renal service rule. The PICC is cancelled; blood is drawn from the back of the right hand, and a short line is placed there.

vitals.plan: “Protect left arm veins” on chart and bed

choices.text: Protect the left arm: draw from the hand or right arm, no PICC unless the attending agrees.
choices.feedback: His non-dominant left arm is the most likely site for a future fistula. Vein preservation is everyone’s job, and the intern can do it today. Write “protect veins” on the chart and the bed.

vitals.plan: “Protect left arm veins” on chart and bed

choices.text: Use the left forearm for today’s blood draw, since the veins are best, but skip the PICC.
choices.feedback: Skipping the PICC is right, but repeated punctures of the left forearm damage the same veins. Use the back of the hand or the other arm.
choices.then: You redirect the draw to the back of the right hand and mark the chart.

vitals.plan: “Protect left arm veins” on chart and bed

n2.prompt: What do you write in the renal plan?

choices.text: He is already admitted: insert a temporary catheter and start hemodialysis before discharge.
choices.feedback: He has no symptoms or signs that call for dialysis. The Initiating Dialysis Early and Late (IDEAL) trial showed no survival benefit from starting early by a number, and a temporary catheter brings infection risk he does not need.
choices.then: The attending reviews the note and changes it: no dialysis now; begin education and preparation.

choices.text: Stable and well. Discuss dialysis when his eGFR falls below 10.
choices.feedback: Waiting until then leaves no time for a fistula to mature, a transplant work-up, a vaccine series or paperwork. That is how planned patients end up starting in the emergency room.
choices.then: The attending asks you to start preparation now, since he has crossed both thresholds.

choices.text: Begin modality education and preparation now; no dialysis today; discuss with the attending.
choices.feedback: These are Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) 2024 practice points, advice without a graded evidence review. Preparation takes months, so it starts on risk, not on the day dialysis begins. A 2-year KFRE risk above 40% and an eGFR below about 15 to 20 both trigger it.

choices.text: Start education, but leave the vaccine, access and transplant steps until he has chosen a modality.
choices.feedback: Education is the first step, but hepatitis B vaccination takes months to complete and is needed whatever he chooses. Start the steps with long lead times now.
choices.then: The attending adds hepatitis B serology and the social worker referral to the plan.

n3.scene: Before discharge, Dr. Manalo explains peritoneal dialysis to Mr. Soriano and Liza with a printed chart in Tagalog. She asks you how to check that it worked.

choices.text: Give them the leaflet in Tagalog, and ask Liza whether her husband understood the steps.
choices.feedback: A leaflet helps, and Liza matters, but asking her about him does not test the explanation. Ask him to explain it himself.
choices.then: Dr. Manalo asks him to explain it in his own words. He thinks the catheter goes in a vein; she corrects it and asks again.

choices.text: Ask him, “Do you understand?” and have Liza sign the education record for both of them.
choices.feedback: That question usually gets a polite yes that hides confusion. It does not test your explanation.
choices.then: He says yes. You suggest she ask him to explain it in his own words; he thinks the catheter goes in a vein, and she corrects it.

choices.text: Ask him to explain the exchanges in his own words, correct, ask again, and write it down.
choices.feedback: Teach-back tests the explanation, not the patient. His answers, and fears such as “once you start dialysis you die soon,” belong in the chart. Record his answer, questions and fears.
choices.then: He thinks the catheter goes in a vein; Dr. Manalo corrects it, and he explains it correctly the second time. He asks whether he could still drive.

n4.scene: A month later the fellow runs a family meeting and asks you to present the options. Liza says she would give him a kidney if she could. Your hospital offers only in-center HD.

choices.text: All four paths, both of them referred for transplant, then ask what a good day looks like.
choices.feedback: KDIGO 2024 asks that every patient hear about all kidney replacement options and conservative care. Transplantation, for those who can receive it, usually offers the most life and freedom, and a willing relative is the reason to refer early. In-center HD, PD at home, transplantation (referring him and Liza to the transplant center) and comprehensive conservative management; ask what a good day would look like a year from now.

vitals.plan: Transplant referral (patient and wife); HD access referral

choices.text: In-center HD, since it is what the hospital offers and PhilHealth covers the sessions.
choices.feedback: Leaving options out is a decision made for the patient. The size of a benefit should never choose the modality.
choices.then: The fellow adds PD, transplantation and conservative care, and asks about Liza’s offer. Both are referred to the transplant center.

vitals.plan: Transplant referral (patient and wife); HD access referral

choices.text: HD and PD now; transplantation can be discussed once he is stable on dialysis.
choices.feedback: Transplant evaluation is long, and a preemptive transplant is best for suitable patients. Waiting until he is on dialysis gives that up.
choices.then: The fellow adds transplantation and conservative care. Both he and Liza are referred to the transplant center.

vitals.plan: Transplant referral (patient and wife); HD access referral

choices.text: All the options, but tell them honestly that transplant is really only for families who can afford Manila.
choices.feedback: Cost and distance are real, but deciding for them ends the conversation. PhilHealth transplant benefits exist; confirm the current rules and let the family weigh it.
choices.then: The fellow corrects the impression and refers both of them to the transplant center.

vitals.plan: Transplant referral (patient and wife); HD access referral

n5.scene: Six months later he chose HD while the transplant work-up continues. His left-arm fistula is maturing. His eGFR is 8, but he has no symptoms. A covering doctor has written: “eGFR 8. Insert temporary catheter and start HD today.”

choices.text: Follow the note: the number is low enough, and starting now avoids an emergency start later.
choices.feedback: A single eGFR never decides alone. KDIGO 2024 advises starting for symptoms or signs, often but not always at a GFR of 5 to 10, and a temporary catheter now would bypass the fistula you planned for.
choices.then: You call the attending, who cancels the catheter and asks you to see him more often instead.

vitals.plan: No start today; monthly visits; symptom list given

choices.text: Discuss with the attending; no start for the number alone; closer visits and written warning signs.
choices.feedback: In IDEAL, a planned early start did not improve survival, and most patients assigned to wait started a little earlier because symptoms appeared. Watch closely and start for the right reasons, on a working access. Ask about appetite, nausea, itch, sleep, concentration, weight and breathlessness each visit.

vitals.plan: No start today; monthly visits; symptom list given

choices.text: Cancel the catheter and see him again in three months, since he has no symptoms of uremia today.
choices.feedback: Not starting is right, but three months is too long at an eGFR of 8. Symptoms, potassium and acidosis need checking at short intervals.
choices.then: The attending shortens the interval to monthly and asks you to give him a list of symptoms to watch for.

vitals.plan: No start today; monthly visits; symptom list given

end.title: The following February
end.text: In January his appetite falls and he develops nausea. He starts hemodialysis in February through his matured fistula, on a day chosen in advance, registered in the PhilHealth Dialysis Database (PDD) beforehand. Liza’s evaluation at the transplant center continues.

debrief:
What this case teaches

  • Protect the veins today. No PICC and no punctures in the likely fistula arm unless the attending agrees.
  • Prepare on risk, start on symptoms. A 2-year KFRE risk above 40% or an eGFR below about 15 to 20 starts preparation (KDIGO 2024 practice points); symptoms and signs, not a number, start dialysis.
  • Use teach-back and record what the patient understood and feared.
  • Present all four paths, including transplantation and conservative care, whether or not your hospital offers them.

See When to start, The options and Preparation.
